speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, I move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head J of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is a story about Dr Goh Keng Swee in the early years of our Independence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When Singapore began building up its armed forces, some thought we were overreacting.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we did not take our own security seriously, no one else would.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we did not prepare early, we would prepare too late.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we did not build strength ourselves, we would depend on the strength of others.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That clarity shaped the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) we know today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He warned that the real danger was not vulnerability but neglect.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without defence, we would drift into becoming a colony or a satellite, exposed to pressure and ransom.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We do not choose the ambitions of larger powers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we choose whether we face reality squarely, prepare seriously and shape our own future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, the global order is entering a more uncertain phase.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The belief that economic integration would soften rivalry has frayed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The assumption that international rules protect small states is under strain.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Major power competition is sharpening across technology, supply chains, energy and data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At the recent Munich Security Conference, the conclusion was sobering.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When sanctions expand, our trade dependent economy feels it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When multilateral forums stall, small states lose room to manoeuvre.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Emerging technologies have lowered the barriers of conflict.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Drones and precision capabilities can offset traditional advantages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Information campaigns can divide societies before a single shot is fired.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It tests energy grids, digital infrastructure and food security.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For hyper connected Singapore, the frontline is no longer distant.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is the phone in a young person's hand, the data centre powering our economy and the port anchoring our supply lines.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Security today demands resilience in systems, clarity in command and confidence in society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, I seek the Minister's update on three fronts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How has that translated into force posture and operational readiness?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we remain trusted by all, yet subordinate to none?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A strong SAF is the bedrock of deterrence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Credible strength deters miscalculation, prevents adventurism and preserves peace.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without this conventional core, deterrence weakens and risk rises.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The contest spans physical, digital and cognitive domains.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled decision support must be embedded from the outset.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The SAF's digital and intelligence arm reflects this shift.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Its value lies in integration, whether sensors and shooters operate as one network, whether commanders share a coherent real time picture, whether decisions are made with speed, discipline and unity of effort.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are we on track in integrating sensors, shooters and digital systems into a unified operational network?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are we building layered defences against unmanned threats around critical infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are acquisition strategies flexible enough to cope with rapid technological cycles and supply chain disruptions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And what is the state of preparation of the SAF for asymmetrical warfare across drone and cyber domains?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our strategic depth is not measured in kilometres.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is measured in foresight, adaptability and resolve, in being early, not late, prepared, not surprised, steady, not reactive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the early years, some thought he was overly cautious.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What looked like over preparation was prudence, what looked like caution was clarity, what looked like pessimism was responsibility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about ensuring that future generations inherit a country that decides for itself.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Dr Goh chose to build this before danger was obvious.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Now it is our turn, our turn to prepare before we are forced to, our turn to build before we are tested, our turn to choose strength over drift, responsibility over dependence, resolve over resignation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we do that, we honour more than his legacy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We ensure that Singapore's future remains decided by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, the global geopolitical environment is becoming increasingly complex and uncertain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Major power competition has sharpened and long-standing institutions are under strain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even alliances, such as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), which have underpinned decades of stability, face questions about cohesion and a potential fracture.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While Singapore is not party to these alliances, any significant shift in the global security environment will inevitably have wider implications.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, I would like to ask about whether MINDEF intends to refine its approach to building defence relations with key partners and if so, how it intends to do that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Within our region, the ASEAN Defence Ministers Meeting (ADMM) and ADMM-Plus bring together the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and key external partners, including China, India, Japan and others, to strengthen dialogue and cooperation in defence and security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Beyond traditional defence cooperation, we already work closely with partners to address transnational threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We also contribute to the Counter Terrorism Information Facility, working alongside like-minded countries to exchange information and provide early warning of potential terrorist plots.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In maritime security, Singapore contributes to the Information Fusion Centre, which facilitates timely information sharing on maritime threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We also participate in coordinated patrols in the Malacca Straits with Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, and support broader international anti-piracy efforts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These practical initiatives demonstrate how defence diplomacy and security cooperation can directly enhance our security and regional stability.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the strategic environment evolves, it may be timely to consider how we can further strengthen and adapt this web of partnerships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Will Singapore explore new partnerships with like-minded nations or find meaningful ways to deepen existing relationships with countries to share our commitment to international law and to dealing with multilateral security frameworks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Are there new areas in which Singapore is looking to collaborate with other countries as well?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Singapore's success as a small nation in a complex world has always depended on one crucial factor – our ability to be trusted by all, while belonging exclusively to no one.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For decades, our strategic value as a neutral convener and reliable partner has served us well.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We have consistently championed international law and multilateral frameworks, signalling to our partners that we can be counted on.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We continue to host the annual Shangri-La Dialogue, where defence ministers from around the world gather for frank discussions on regional security.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We have facilitated trilateral exchanges between major powers, proving our professionalism and discretion on the global stage.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, the rapidly changing security landscape presents a new challenge to sustaining this position.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Great power competition is intensifying at an unprecedented pace.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Nations are increasingly pressured to choose sides and the middle ground that Singapore has traditionally occupied is shrinking.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We also face new threats that straddle the space between peace and conflict.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Such hybrid warfare tactics make neutrality more difficult to define and maintain.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: On top of these, technological warfare and cyber threats transcend traditional diplomatic boundaries while economic interdependence creates new vulnerabilities that adversaries can exploit.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As a small nation, maintaining our value proposition is not merely advantageous, it is existential.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Unlike larger powers that can rely on military might or economic leverage, Singapore's security depends on our ability to remain relevant and trusted by major stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Given this, I would like to ask how MINDEF/SAF plans to maintain its relevance and value proposition amidst the evolving security landscape.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Apart from preserving our reputation as a key and trusted partner, are there new ways in which we can demonstrate our value-add to others?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, the world has entered a new era of conflict, one that is more complex, more contested and more technologically driven than anything we have witnessed in generations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What makes this moment particularly consequential is not just the number of conflicts, but how they are being fought.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, emerging technologies such as AI, quantum computing, advanced robotics and cyber warfare capabilities are reshaping the character of conflict – how wars are fought, who fights them and where the battlefield lies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These technologies blur the traditional boundaries between military and civilian domains.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Civilian infrastructure, businesses and everyday technology become legitimate targets.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In our context, ordinary Singaporeans, especially the vulnerable, could be put directly in harm's way.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have already seen how these new capabilities have made their way into recent conflicts and changed the way they are fought and won.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Commercial drones – the kind any of us might be able to buy online – can be fitted with AI and turned into precision weapons.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They can be coordinated in swarms that may overwhelm even sophisticated air defence systems.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Meanwhile, cyberattacks are achieving what once required bombs and missiles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They can shut down power grids, cripple communications and spread false information to damage public morale.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Modern sensors can now see through clouds, track movements in real-time and provide commanders with battlefield awareness that was unimaginable a decade ago.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the Russia-Ukraine war, both sides deploy drones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The digital domain has become a full-fledged theatre of conflict.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is most worrying is that these technologies are no longer exclusive to states.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even non-state groups can now access capabilities that were once the preserve of major military powers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a highly connected, technology-dependent city-state, the very systems that drive our economic success also create vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our concentrated urban environment means that attacks using these technologies could have devastating effects.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore can leverage these same technologies to enhance our capabilities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our strong technology sector and culture of innovation position us well to develop and deploy emerging technologies for defence purposes, potentially strengthening our defence partnerships in the process.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But staying ahead will require not only technological innovation but also a willingness to continually adapt.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to constantly monitor technological developments, assess their military potential and anticipate how adversaries might use them against us.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Mr Chairman, as a former military service personnel, war is more salient for me than most in this House.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In a recent moving speech at the Kranji War memorial, Senior Minister of State Murali reminded us that "peace is hard won, that war is not a story of the past, but a reality of the present" and that "today, the world is not at peace – a few countries are already at war, others are preparing for it and still others know they must." Singapore has been in a state of preparedness for all the years of our independence.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But the nature of war is fast changing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Today, unmanned solutions are at the forefront of conflicts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The ongoing war in Ukraine has demonstrated their cost effectiveness dramatically.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Looking ahead, can I ask the Minister three related points on manpower, security and supply chain?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: What are some examples of unmanned technologies development strategies or trajectories in the next 10 to 20 years that can truly replace human operators?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Can remote unmanned technologies truly fly aircraft, drive tanks and launch bridges?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We ought, of course, to avoid a situation where we own many unmanned systems but in the end, manpower needs are not very much reduced.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Also, in terms of the split between manned and unmanned defence systems, in terms of capex investment, what is rough proportion now and what will it be in the future?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The same benefits that help us project war can just as easily be used against us.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This dual nature of unmanned technology means we must be both users and defenders against these systems.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: How does SAF ensure high availability and reliability of unmanned systems, especially on cybersecurity attacks?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Third, as we expand our unmanned capabilities, we must also consider supply chain resilience.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Over-reliance on any single source or region for these critical systems could create vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Chairman, as a digital nation, Singapore's strength has also become our vulnerability.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We rely heavily on online infrastructure for almost everything in our daily lives: communications, government services, banking, healthcare and commerce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This digital interconnectedness brings tremendous convenience and productivity, but without robust safeguards, it also exposes us to significant systemic risks.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: What concerns me most is how cyberattacks can directly disrupt the lives of ordinary Singaporeans, especially our most vulnerable communities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We have seen globally how attacks on power grids and critical infrastructure can trigger widespread blackouts, affecting hospitals where patients depend on life support systems, transport networks that workers rely on, and schools where our children learn.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: On the military front, the stakes are even higher.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Cyberattacks can disrupt command and control systems, compromise intelligence and surveillance operations, and undermine the functionality of critical defence platforms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In a crisis, digital paralysis can translate into operational disadvantages.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The pace of technological change is rapid and relentless.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Emerging technologies, including AI-enabled cyber tools are reshaping the threat landscape.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It is therefore imperative that the SAF continuously adapts to stay ahead of evolving digital threats.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: How will these efforts further enhance Singapore's overall cyber defence resilience as part of a whole-of-nation approach?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, as a small nation, we have always lived with one hard truth – we cannot count on others to defend Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That is why from our earliest years, we invested heavily in building a credible SAF and why defence has always been treated as a long-term business, not an annual shopping list.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It takes years to develop capabilities, train people and build up infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And today's security environment is becoming more complex, with cyber threats, disinformation and hybrid tactics that target our systems and our social cohesion, even without a single shot fired.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I agree – where necessary, we must invest in new capabilities to keep the SAF agile and resilient.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But at the same time, we owe it to Singaporeans to be prudent.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Every dollar for defence is also a dollar not spent on other pressing priorities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: People say it is healthcare, education, cost-of-living support and strengthening our social compact.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In that regard, I have two questions for the Minister.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, what stronger "value-for-money" checks are in place?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How do we manage cost over-runs and lifecycle costs, and how do we retire or refresh legacy systems, so that we do not carry capabilities that no longer match today's threat landscape?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, Singaporeans support defence spending when it is clearly tied to real capabilities and disciplined stewardship.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our commitment must remain – strong security, but with strong accountability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Similarly, Taiwan reportedly faces a backlog exceeding US$21 billion, with delivery timelines of fighter aircraft and coastal defence systems slipping repeatedly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Robust procurement budgets cannot purchase security if hardware remains on a distant assembly line.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therein lies the risk of a capability vacuum, if our own high-end platforms do not arrive on time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The operational life of existing assets is not infinite.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We cannot afford a security hiatus where our surveillance or ratal defence posture is compromised, because we are waiting in a global queue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Relying on a single source for critical high-end systems may create a strategic vulnerability amidst current global instability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore must be a partner with sufficient leverage to demand delivery certainty for every asset.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, MINDEF must ensure that multi-billion-dollar high-end contracts are transparent and accountable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can be done by ensuring the Auditor-General's Office (AGO) is given full access to audit procurement milestones, contract variations and delivery timelines.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Mr Chairman, National Service (NS) is the bedrock of our defence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Every generation of Singaporeans has served and every generation deserves to know that their time in uniform is used to its fullest.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Are we deploying our national servicemen as meaningfully as we can and are the skills they bring being optimised?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, enlistees arrive with increasingly diverse capabilities – from digital skills to technical trades, logistics experience, language abilities and even food and beverage (F&B) or retail operations knowledge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: How is MINDEF strengthening the identification and deployment of such capabilities, so that NS becomes not just a duty fulfilled but a period of genuine contribution to our defence?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I would also ask MINDEF to consider greater flexibility during NS.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can we explore Work-Learn schemes that allow servicemen, where operationally feasible, to build career-relevant credentials along their services?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can early enlistment options be made available for those who wish to enter NS before the standard window, giving young men more agency over how they sequence education, service and work?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For our Operationally Ready National Servicemen (NSmen), I hope MINDEF will look into more structured Expertise Deployment – matching reservists to roles that draw on competencies from their civilian lives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A reservist who is a mechanic, a nurse or a logistics coordinator should be contributing where his skills matter most.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I look forward to MINDEF's update on how we can make every hour of service count.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Kenneth Tiong, you may take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Does the DIS have the talent pipeline fight the next breach?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These are genuine efforts and I acknowledge them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But the expertise to detect zero-day exploits in network firewalls to identify custom root kits, like MOPSLED and REPTILE, to trace state sponsored command and control infrastructure routed through commercial cloud services, this is predominantly in the private sector at firms, like Cloudstrike, Mandiant, Palo Alto Networks.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The response operation Cyber Guardian required coordination across six agencies precisely because no single entity, including DIS, had sufficient depth alone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Minister acknowledged last September that military and civilian cyber threats are increasingly blurred.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But if the threat landscape is blurred, the talent pipeline should be too.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Our programmes train soldiers to become cyber defenders.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We do not seem to have a dedicated pathway for cyber professionals to become soldiers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Military service carries entry requirements designed for conventional soldiering – fitness standards, ten weeks of basic training, rigid career tracks and compensation that cannot compete with industry.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These are appropriate for infantry, but perhaps counterproductive for recruiting a 40-year-old penetration tester.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Last year, the United Kingdom (UK) launched the Cyber Direct entry scheme, a fast-track pathway for civilians into military cyber roles.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The first cohort of 30 entered operational roles in late 2025, helping defend UK networks against 90,000 attacks over two years.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will MINDEF consider a cyber direct entry pathway for DIS, allowing mid-career industry professionals to serve in military cyber defence with adapted entry requirements and competitive compensation?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Cyber Guardian shows what DIS achieves when it mobilises whole-of-Government.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The next step is to draw from whole of industry.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Despite nominal increases, NSF purchasing power has fallen.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In Budget 2026, the Government announced it will raise the local qualifying salary to $1,800.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Every worker earning that amount receives Central Provident Fund (CPF) as a matter of law.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A second-year NSF corporal in a combat vocation earns $1,035 a month with zero CPF.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If $1,800 is the floor for every worker in Singapore, surely it is the floor for every soldier.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In 2024, my colleague Mr Gerald Giam proposed raising NSF allowances to at least the local qualifying salary of $1,600 with CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How replied that NS is a duty, not employment, but SAF Regulars serve the same duty with market salaries and full CPF.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If duty and employment were mutually exclusive, we could not have a professional army.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: By their second year, NSFs are fully trained and operationally deployed, manning posts, running day to day operations, performing similar tasks as Regulars.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Chairman, NS is fundamental to Singapore's defence and continued prosperity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NS is a rite of passage, where young Singaporean men will have to take on the serious responsibility of contributing to our nation’s defence.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During my years serving in the Singapore Police Force and also in my earlier years doing my National Service in the SAF, I have met many national servicemen with a wide variety of skills.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Through diverse vocations, ranging from logistics and engineering to cybersecurity and communications, our servicemen develop both hard and soft skills that are transferable to their civilian lives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They gain technical expertise, leadership skills and problem-solving abilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They also learn to work under pressure, manage resources efficiently and get along with diverse teams across different backgrounds and cultures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, Mr Chairman, I have a concern about what happens after our national servicemen complete their service.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is one thing for their commanders and superiors to recognise their growth and achievements through awards and various forms of NS-related recognition.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But what is more crucial and what will affect these young men's career prospects is whether their future employers will recognise their practical skills that they have acquired during NS.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We need to ensure that employers can make a more holistic assessment on their employability, one that accounts for the skills and experience that they gain during their NS.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To that end, how does MINDEF intend to ensure that the skills acquired by servicemen are duly recognised?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Chairman, peace and prosperity is neither natural nor permanent.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: How do these partnerships enhance the SAF's operational readiness while maintaining strategic flexibility?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: What safeguards are in place to ensure that we do not become overly reliant to any single defence partnership?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Chairman, our external partnerships are only as strong as our internal resilience.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Some people I met asked why commitment to Total Defence and NS remains relevant.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singaporeans must view Total Defence and NS as investments in our collective future, not burdensome obligations as how some may have painted.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: So, how can we harmonise aspirations, work and life as well as service and commitment and duty?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Total Defence and NS goes beyond domestic policies – both are strategic assets, enhancing our value as a defence partner.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: When other countries know Singapore has citizens who participate in national defence across all demographics, and a society that can withstand various pressures, it signals serious business.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Beyond military training – it embodies collective commitment to sovereignty and shared responsibility for the nation's future.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: When NSFs contribute meaningfully to Singapore's defence, their contributions become part of a larger shared commitment to safeguard our families, communities and our way of life.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It is therefore key for Singaporeans, servicemen and Significant Others to appreciate its intent.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: At its core, Total Defence recognises that every Singaporean – regardless of race, language and religion – has a part to play in building a strong, secure and cohesive nation.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We saw Total Defence in action during the SARS and COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It demonstrated how coordinated Government responses, economic support measures, social solidarity and digital solutions can work together to manage national emergencies.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: When households participate in Total Defence exercises, they are not just preparing for emergencies at a personal level, they are building a wider foundation of community resilience.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: However, more needs to be done to help Singaporeans see these connections and understand how their participation strengthens our defence and social fabric.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We need greater community engagement that reaches all segments of our society, including elderly residents, new citizens and families from different backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We must ensure that Total Defence activities are accessible and meaningful to everyone, regardless of their circumstances.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: What integration modules, multilingual resources or community initiatives are available to equip these segments with practical crisis response and knowledge?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Ensuring that everyone who calls Singapore home understands their role will strengthen our collective resilience.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Not just hardware but also mindset, cohesion and shared responsibility.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: If we are entering a more dangerous world, our greatest strategic asset will not only be a strong SAF, but a society that understands what is at stake and stands ready to defend it.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In our national language, Sir, bersatu kita teguh.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   Defence is not merely a military issue.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It concerns whether a nation can survive, whether society has confidence and whether we can continue to function normally when facing external shocks.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, the international situation is becoming increasingly unstable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Conflicts and tensions are no longer short-term events, but seem to be a permanent backdrop.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For an open small state like Singapore, risks will not come from just one direction, but may simultaneously affect transport corridors, energy and food supplies, as well as the stability of financial and digital systems.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Traditional military threats still exist, but more apparent is the increase in cross-domain risks.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and attacks on critical infrastructure can all occur during peacetime, with significant effects.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Security is no longer just in the battlefield but encompasses the entire social system.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The development of artificial intelligence, unmanned systems and cyber capabilities is enabling countries to enhance their military capabilities faster.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For small states with limited resources, we must be clearer about what matters most – we cannot do everything.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I hope to understand the future priorities more clearly, so I have questions in four areas for the Minister to clarify.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When risks span multiple domains, no single department can respond alone.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When facing cross-domain shocks, how do we ensure clear decision-making and smooth coordination to maintain social stability and confidence?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My concern is the overall architecture and MINDEF's future role positioning.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Technology investment must be far-sighted; we cannot blindly chase short-term trends.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Minister, over the next 10 to 20 years, how do we determine the most important capabilities?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How do we ensure that technological development synchronises with operational concepts, rather than merely updating equipment?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, with technology changing so rapidly, how do we maintain local research and development capabilities?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How do we establish long-term, stable cooperative relationships between research institutions, enterprises and defence needs, rather than just doing short-term projects?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For a small state's defence, people are key.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Technology can improve efficiency, but talent determines how far we can go.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Minister, what kind of talent structure do we need for the future?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Particularly for science and technology and engineering talent, what role do they play in our defence?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How do we enable more local talent to see clear development pathways and be willing to commit long term?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, whilst strengthening highly skilled teams, how do we continue to consolidate the social cohesion and shared sense of responsibility brought by NS?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that defence spending needs to be stable, because capability building cannot change year by year.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But we also face pressures from an ageing population and increasing social expenditure.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Minister, under the premise of fiscal sustainability, how does MINDEF clearly explain long-term planning and prioritisation to Parliament?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How do we ensure resources are concentrated on key capabilities, and through more systematic assessment, improve efficiency and effectiveness?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, security is not a momentary issue, but a responsibility to the next generation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The goal of defence is to ensure that Singapore maintains stability, autonomy and resilience in an era full of uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Only when a nation is strong, can it stand independently in the world.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: NS as an institution has already evolved beyond protection and the defence of Singapore, but also as a social fabric for us to bond together, to understand each other, whether it is race or culture.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the compulsory services, we also have the SAF Volunteer Corps (SAFVC), SPF's Volunteer Special Constabulary and Citizens on Patrol.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: At SCDF, we have the Company Emergency Response Team.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: If we can do that, then I think we will be able to build a much more cohesive society that people who are not male citizens serving in the compulsory service, females or new citizens can then claim they are serving their NS.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Tonight, I am going to walk up and down the Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats, the HDB car parks.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I think that is also contribution to the protection and defence of the community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, recent conflicts overseas remind us that national defence is not carried by the military alone.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Ukraine, ordinary citizens have played important roles, countering misinformation, supporting one another and sustaining national morale even under prolonged crisis.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These experiences underscore an enduring lesson – resilience ultimately rests on the preparedness and resolve of the whole society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But behind every capable armed force is a population that understands the risks it faces and is prepared to respond collectively when crisis happen.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In Singapore, building such preparedness begins with awareness.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many Singaporeans have grown up in peace and stability, and as a result, security threats can sometimes feel distant or abstract.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Strengthening national resilience therefore requires continued efforts to deepen public understanding of why defence matters and how every segment of society has a role to play.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MINDEF and the SAF have laid strong foundations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Total Defence education in schools and NS remain central pillars of our defence system.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For many Singaporeans, NS is where responsibility, teamwork and commitment to country become tangible realities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, opportunities exist to broaden engagement across society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Women, who make up half our population, may wish to contribute beyond supporting family members in service.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Likewise, young people, new citizens and others may be keen but uncertain about how they can meaningfully participate in strengthening national resilience.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask three clarifications.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, how does MINDEF envision the role of the wider population evolving within Singapore's defence ecosystem over the longer term, particularly as demographics change and fewer citizens may have direct experience of NS?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, beyond preparedness exercises and participation schemes, how is MINDEF working across the Government and society to ensure that, in a national crisis, Singapore can mobilise quickly with public trust, cohesion and shared resolve already in place?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, as the nature of conflict evolves beyond conventional warfare to include hybrid, informational and societal dimensions, how is MINDEF strengthening Singapore's overall whole-of-nation resilience framework so that our defence posture remains credible not only militarily, but also socially and psychologically?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Volunteers undergo rigorous training to ensure they are ready to take on responsibilities that support operations and training.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Above all, the SAFVC reflects the spirit of shared duty of ordinary people stepping forward in extraordinary ways.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Each volunteer strengthens our defence network and reinforces the message that keeping Singapore safe is a collective responsibility.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Last year marked a meaningful milestone for our defence community, SAFVC.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Their commitment reminds us that contributing to defence extends well beyond National Service obligations.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: It is a shared responsibility anchored in values, trust and the willingness to step up.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: From the outset, SAF was built on a powerful idea – to give more people an avenue to contribute to national defence and deepen the understanding of what it takes to keep Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: These experiences sharpen skills, builds confidence and deepens appreciation of the complex behind-the-scenes work that keeps our nation secure.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: We should recognise the sacrifice our volunteers make.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Many juggle careers and family responsibilities while serving.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Internationally, Singapore is not alone in engaging civilians in defence.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Estonia's Cyber Defence League mobilises IT professionals to help protect national cyber infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: In the UK and Australia, the army reserve harnesses civilian expertise through more formal military structures, enabling citizens to contribute while maintaining their civilian careers.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: These models reaffirm the value of flexible pathways that connect civilian skills to defence needs.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: If we continue to train progressively, deploy meaningfully and recognise generously, we will keep strengthening a defence ecosystem where every capable pair of hands and every willing heart can contribute to Singapore's security.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It has been the home away from camp for our national servicemen.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On a personal note, I have seen how these spaces have evolved.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Since my younger days, SAFRA Tampines was where I headed to for a game of squash or badminton and my regular swims.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, I see national servicemen bringing their toddlers to the enrichment centres and their elderly parents to the restaurants.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: SAFRA has successfully mirrored the life stages of our servicemen, moving from a space for the boys to a space for the family.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The last time I popped into SAFRA was at SAFRA Tampines again, but with my son, for bowling; and recently, in December, for a joint community event between my Pioneer Coordinating Arts and Culture Club and SAFRA Jurong.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While the new Choa Chu Kang clubhouse is a masterpiece of modern integration, our NSFs and pre-enlistees have different digital and social habits compared to my generation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Specifically, how will SAFRA ensure that its offerings remain bespoke for different segments, from the pre-enlistee looking for fitness prep, to the NSF seeking respite, to the former national serviceman who still wishes to maintain that link to the SAF fraternity?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We are no longer just looking at borders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We are looking at hybrid threats – misinformation, cyberattacks and threats to our social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: SAFRA's vision is for every national serviceman to be committed to Total Defence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But in a hybrid world, the commitment of the national serviceman alone is not enough.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need the commitment of the entire public.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Public support is the "fuel" for our defence engine.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is what makes the "whole-of-society" mentality possible.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If the public does not understand the why behind our defence spending or the sacrifice of our servicemen, our national resilience weakens.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But I believe SAFRA's expertise in community building is a really untapped resource for broader national engagement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Are there plans to use SAFRA as a platform where non-servicemen – could be spouses, children and new citizens – so that they can better appreciate the contributions of our NSmen and learn how they too can play a part in Total Defence?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By opening SAFRA's "doors", both physical and metaphorical wider, we do not just celebrate our soldiers; we strengthen our society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And it is about whether every Singaporean understands his or her stake in this country and appreciates the role that NS plays in keeping Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But without sustained community support and identification with the institution of NS, our defence posture will gradually hollow out.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As our society continues to evolve and becomes more prosperous and comfortable, defence concerns can easily slip to the back of our minds.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Families today juggle work pressures, children’s education, caregiving for elderly parents and of course, rising costs of living.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Young professionals are focused on career advancement and personal aspirations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is natural that defence issues do not feature prominently in daily conversation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The peace and stability we have enjoyed for decades also make existential threats feel distant.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is precisely why community institutions matter more now than ever.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They bridge the gap between our defence needs and everyday life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They keep defence awareness alive in spaces where Singaporeans already gather.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has clubhouses across the island and a large membership base.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is where national servicemen meet friends, where families send their children for classes, where people exercise, dine and unwind.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have personally spent time at SAFRA facilities with my family as many Members would have.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are ordinary moments, but they are also opportunities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Around us are NSmen who have trained together, served together and carry stories of hardship, camaraderie and pride.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We hear conversations about friendships forged in outfield conditions, about the satisfaction of completing a demanding exercise, about the quiet pride in wearing the uniform and doing one's part.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And, of course, when national servicemen meet, complain about tough training as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They remind us that security is not an abstract idea.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is built by sons, daughters, brothers, sisters, fathers, colleagues.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My question therefore is how MINDEF can deepen partnerships with organisations like SAFRA so that they go beyond just being facilities for recreation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would there be plans to develop programmes within these community platforms that will actively foster inter-generational understanding of NS?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, perhaps dialogues where veterans and younger Singaporeans can share perspectives on NS, preparedness workshops that involve entire families, activities that integrate the messages of Total Defence into everyday community life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How can SAFRA and similar institutions better engage not only our NSmen, but also spouses, their children and our new citizens as well?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many new Singaporeans may not have grown up with NS is a formative experience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, their sense of belonging and commitment is equally important for us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can these platforms help them understand our defence story and feel invested in protecting their newly adopted home?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ultimately, defence in the community should be visible in small but telling ways.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Parents who instinctively teach their children resilience and preparedness, neighbours who check on one another during crises, young Singaporeans who see NS not merely as an obligation, but as a shared rite of passage, and new citizens who speak of Singapore's security as their responsibility as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we are intentional in leveraging the reach and influence of institutions like SAFRA, we can ensure that Total Defence can remain a lived national commitment and not confined to the uniformed services or to our schools.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would appreciate if the Ministry could share what outcomes MINDEF will track to assess whether defence is truly anchored in the community and what more can be done to strengthen this vital pillar of national resilience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's Total Defence framework has always recognised that a strong defence system is multi-faceted and goes beyond the military.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The six pillars of defence include, the military, civil, economic, social, digital and psychological defence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: To this end, while belabouring the point, I would like to join my Parliamentary colleagues, Mr Patrick Tay, and my only namesake in the House Mr Alex Yam, to speak about SAFRA.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: SAFRA National Service Association is a familiar and accessible platform for NSmen, their families and the wider community to come together to participate in Total Defence activities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: With its strong infrastructure and extensive member network, I believe more can be done to mobilise this platform.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: SAFRA's extensive network of members and suite of infrastructure, present a wealth of resource and opportunities for us to leverage.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, I would like to ask the Minister whether MINDEF have plans to better leverage SAFRA's existing infrastructure and network to build stronger ties and raise Total Defence awareness in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chair, let me first thank Members for their interest and support for MINDEF and SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chair, we live in unprecedented and increasingly dangerous times.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Yet, Singapore has enjoyed another year of relative peace and economic prosperity.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We do not, should not and must not take this for granted.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Even if we had been lucky, luck favours only the prepared.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The world, as Members have said, is undergoing rapid and disruptive structural changes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many of our old assumptions about the world and how it works are less or no longer relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To secure our place in the world, we must anticipate, adapt and develop capabilities ahead of time, to pre-empt the new threats and developments, even as we continue to manage the existing and enduring ones.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If we fail, we risk irrelevance and heightened insecurity.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These immutable truths have set the foundations for our approach to defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We do not have the option of falling back and regrouping to come back from an attack.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our lifelines go through other countries' air and sea space to reach international space to connect with the world.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We cannot allow ourselves to be physically and digitally cut-off from the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Therefore, we have built the SAF and developed operational concepts to overturn these vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our lack of domestic resources also makes us susceptible to external disruptions, because we rely on international trade to sustain ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To overcome this limitation, we must strengthen our resilience to withstand and outlast any pressure from external forces.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is not just an SAF responsibility but a whole-of-society effort through Total Defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond numbers, we must also be able to harness and deploy our whole-of-nation talent effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It has become clear that the longstanding norms that have governed international relations have reached a turning point.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singapore and much of the world have benefitted from the multilateral rules-based order.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This order prioritised collective problem-solving and rules of behaviour in the global commons, as well as serving as guardrails against military escalation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, we can no longer expect countries to work within international laws and norms as a default.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Rules that once restrained behaviours are being tested and, in some cases, deliberately ignored.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When norms erode, behaviours become unpredictable, leading to greater insecurity in the global environment.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is in such times, more than ever, that we need a strong and capable defence to secure our national interests.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On the international stage, Singapore must also make clear our value proposition so that we remain a relevant and valued partner.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While conventional conflict has not gone away, what continues to change is how else conflict can be conducted.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The first dimension is the ongoing technological disruption, which has transformed the speed, scale and cost of conventional conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Take drones as an example which many Members have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The rapid tech development cycle today has ramped up the pace of innovation in drone technology, making them more accessible and faster to operationalise as a capability for offence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: What once required advanced and costly military platforms can now sometimes be achieved more quickly and at lower cost by integrating commercial off-the-shelf drone systems with AI.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In Ukraine, we have already seen how drones are scaled and weaponised to inflict disproportionate damage on a bigger and stronger aggressor.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: While these technologies present challenges, they also present opportunities for resource-deficient countries to use them to complement conventional platforms and sensors.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The second dimension is the spectrum on which conflict occurs.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Threat actors no longer need to resort to war to achieve their outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Instead, we are seeing more hostile actions taken along the entire spectrum from peace to war.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And as we have said before, we are not exactly at peace; neither are we at war.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, cyber and digital tools are increasingly preferred by state and non-state actors to exert pressure just short of full-scale war.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As a highly digital country, we have a large surface area of attack as our systems are tightly coupled.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This deep integration also means that the lines between civilian and military targets are blurred, and we are no strangers to such tactics being deployed against us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Such tactics are designed to induce pressure on their targets while mitigating the chances of triggering full-scale military responses, as it is always difficult to attribute responsibility.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They also exploit legal and operational ambiguities that could delay responses.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ultimately, these attacks create uncertainty and seek to undermine confidence and disrupt our society’s ways of life.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In the face of these wide-ranging challenges, how can we continue to defend Singapore and protect our way of life?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must therefore devote attention and resources to our security and relevance and to stand on our own feet.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To Mr Yip Hon Weng’s question, let me highlight our four-pronged approach to tackle the challenges we face: capabilities, commitment, contributions and connections.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, capabilities for the SAF to be a credible armed force.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A well-equipped SAF is one that can defend Singapore against a spectrum of threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As the ultimate backstop for war, the SAF must have robust conventional capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Having robust conventional capabilities remains core to a strong and credible deterrence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must continue to modernise and upgrade them to keep pace with the threats around us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This supports the SAF’s mission in safeguarding Singapore’s Sea Lines of Communication as part of Singapore’s maritime security surveillance network.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The SAF will also continue to scale the use of unmanned platforms for new concepts of operations and pair them with manned platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If I may just make a point here.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many Members have talked about unmanned platforms. "Unmanned platforms" does not mean it does not require manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I always thought that a more appropriate term is “remotely piloted platforms” in scale or individually.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They need manpower, they need different types of manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Navy’s Victory-class Multi-Role Combat Vessel (MRCV) will be equipped with the combat capability of a modern frigate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But it will also be a “mothership” for unmanned systems.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Poh Li San’s point, beyond the conventional, the rise of cheap-asymmetric capabilities, including drones, will present both threats and opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The SAF will develop a “high-low” mix of capabilities, complementing high-end conventional systems with cheap, dual-use systems available in the commercial market, especially in the drone and digital areas.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also be focusing our efforts to integrate both manned and unmanned operations as a system.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As to the mix between manned and unmanned, that will be a dynamic equilibrium determined by the rate of technological progress.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, we can use low-cost naval swarm drones for maritime security.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This builds agility in our processes so that we can rapidly adapt to the changing battlefield and technological landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As we speak today, we already have unmanned surface vessels patrolling the Singapore Straits together with our manned or crewed vessels.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are also cognisant that beyond manned and unmanned systems, modern warfare is also a contest of resilience, and this is where we will also increase our efforts to make sure that our systems are resilient as a whole.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also respond to threats emanating from cheaper unmanned platforms in a way that does not pose significant cost asymmetry.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In other words, we cannot use a missile to take down every drone that comes at us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked about beyond the physical hardware, what else must we do?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must also continue focusing on building our capabilities in the cyber domain.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must keep pace with the rapidly evolving technology and threats that we encounter daily.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To do so, we must continue to experiment and innovate our cyber training practices.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond training our cyber defenders, CyTEC will be equipped with cutting-edge technologies to facilitate innovation and strengthen our cybersecurity.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Like other professional armed forces around the world, SAF does not disclose every capability we develop or deploy.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: What I can say is that the SAF will continue to invest in capabilities ahead of future threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This will give us the decisive edge and allow us to overcome our security challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The SAF will continue to announce our acquisitions at a time of our choosing when such disclosures are operationally useful.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: So far, I have spoken about technology and hard capabilities, which are critical force multipliers for SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Yet beyond and behind each capability is our people, and it is equally important that the SAF trains our people for a much more complex environment.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, we will strengthen our soldiering fundamentals of live-firing and better prepare them against future threats and a wider range of operational scenarios.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Since 2013, the Multi Mission Range Complex (MMRC) at Pasir Laba has been used by generations of NSmen to hone their marksmanship.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Beyond just increased capacity, MMRC 2 will allow our soldiers to train more realistically and precisely across more scenarios and different domains via the new Video Targetry System and MMRC 2 will also allow our soldiers to hone their counter drone techniques.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And it has always been my own personal vision that our NSmen can go into a range to hone their skill, just as they go to a bowling alley.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have and we will continue to invest steadily in conventional, cheap-asymmetric, cyber and classified capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will also train our people well to maximise their capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will focus not only on the "teeth" in terms of the inducting new weapon system, but also on the "tail" in terms of improving resilience of our supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must strive to develop capabilities for the next bound instead of the last conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Adaptation and agility must be built into the SAF DNA.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We do not want to be caught in a situation where we are fundamentally surprised by developments that we should have seen coming.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The task of building up the SAF is never-ending.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must continue to stay ahead of the changing threat landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I am happy to report to the House that when I returned to MINDEF last year, I continued to see this spirit.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In 1997, then a Major Chan Chun Sing was writing about the use of unmanned drones in swarms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We were talking about computer viruses because, for those of you who remember WordPerfect, some of you will know that you can play aircraft simulation if you know the correct code behind WordPerfect.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This has already told us what could come many years later.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In 2000, before I left SAF, we were talking about classified projects that, today, are coming to fruition when I returned to MINDEF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I am glad that today when I returned to SAF, I am seeing my men and women of SAF, not just the talking and thinking about the challenges today, but what are the challenges that could emerge in 10 or 20 years' time.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: That is and that must be the spirit of SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, our defence capability, in my mind, must be manifested in six arms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In our quest for resilience and to strengthen our ability to scale at speed, we must also have a strong and reliable local defence industry.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Their credible capabilities also allow us to be a partner of choice for others to want to work with us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For the second "c", let me touch on the commitments to Singapore's defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This commitment by our political leadership and whole of society is expressed in various forms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To Dr Wan Rizal's point, our first commitment is a steady, consistent and disciplined way that we approach our defence expenditure.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Various Members have asked about how we apply our resources judiciously and apply them in a disciplined way.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This was supposed to be an answer that I will give to Ms Valerie Lee, who has posed a Parliamentary Question, but I thought it is perhaps useful for me to share my seven golden rules of defence expenditure and how we spend money.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Rule number one, operational needs first and last.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our top priority always goes to our operational needs, both current and emerging.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, we must be clear-eyed on our life-cycle cost.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We plan our investment with full consideration of life-cycle cost and long-term sustainability, taking into account the financial and manpower resources needed in acquiring, establishing, developing and maintaining that capability.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We acquire and develop capabilities not in isolation, but with a view towards them being a part of the larger integrated system within SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This ensures that the SAF's capability is more than the sum of its individual parts.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As developing integrated systems and real capabilities take time and consistent effort, we invest steadily in technology and our people's skills and competencies over the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We eschew a feast and famine approach to defence spending.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It is important for SAF to build resilience against disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We achieve this through means such as the ability to adapt to our unique needs, ensuring adequate stockpile and having alternative sources of supplies.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We acquire the most cost-effective system to meet our operational needs, guided by robust professional assessment, rather than being tied to any single source or solution.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Where we need to achieve greater resilience or customise to our own unique needs, we may develop our own unique systems.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Rule number seven, last but not least, goes back to the first – operational needs, always.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our operational needs remain our foremost and utmost consideration so that we can build a strong SAF, equip our war fighters with the best systems available against today's and tomorrow's challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next is our commitment to NS, which is essential for generating the force required to meet our critical needs for national security and survival.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The service and support of our NSFs and NSmen are vital to this effort.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
